title: IB Mandarin B Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them
summary: IB Mandarin B common mistakes can cost easy marks. Learn to read command terms, include units and evidence, manage timing, and practise effectively.
body_markdown:
A Mandarin B student can know the vocabulary, understand the text, and still lose marks.


Imagine a student named Lina. She walks into the exam prepared. She has revised the[five core themes of IB Chinese B](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/the-five-core-themes-of-ib-chinese-b-explained) , memorised useful structures, and completed several writing tasks. Yet when the paper is returned, the losses are painfully ordinary. She explained when the question asked her to identify. She copied a relevant sentence without showing which detail answered the question. She wrote “三十” but omitted “分钟.” Then she spent too long perfecting an early response and rushed the final section.


Lina is hypothetical, but the pattern is familiar. Many IB Mandarin B common mistakes come from execution rather than a complete lack of knowledge. The practical fix is to train three habits: decode the instruction, provide exactly the evidence requested, and control time deliberately.


### The quick mistake-prevention checklist


Before submitting an answer, ask:


- What does the command term require me to do?
- How many points or details are requested?
- Does a number need a unit such as 元, 公里, 点 or 分钟?
- Have I supplied evidence rather than a vague interpretation?
- Does my answer match the expected text type, audience and purpose?
- Am I spending time in proportion to the available marks?
- Have I left enough time to check characters, particles and unanswered items?


This checklist is simple by design. Under pressure, complicated systems tend to disappear. Reliable routines survive.


A student holds an elaborate key while overlooking a simple pull handle on a small box


*The hardest-looking solution is not always the one the question requested.*


### Misreading command terms


The first avoidable error happens before the student writes anything. A question asks for one kind of response, but the student produces another.


If the instruction asks you to identify or state, a brief and precise answer may be enough. If it asks you to explain, your response needs a reason, relationship or mechanism. If it asks for evidence, you must connect your conclusion to a specific detail from the source. The exact wording and acceptable response format depend on the question, so follow the instructions printed on the paper rather than relying on a memorised formula.


Lina’s mistake would be answering the topic she expected instead of the task she actually received. This also appears in writing. A student may produce sophisticated Mandarin but choose an unsuitable format or tone. A public speech, informal message and formal letter do not communicate in the same way. RevisionDojo’s guide to[common Chinese B Paper 1 text types](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-ib-chinese-b-paper-1-text-types-and-how-to-master-them) can help you distinguish their conventions.


### The fix: translate the task into an action


Before answering, mentally reduce the command to a verb:


- **Identify:** name the relevant detail.
- **Describe:** give the important features.
- **Explain:** show why or how.
- **Compare:** address both similarities and differences where required.
- **Justify:** make a claim and support it with relevant evidence.


Underline or circle the instruction during practice if your school permits annotation in that assessment. Then count the requested elements. “Give two reasons” needs two distinct reasons, not one reason expressed twice.


### Omitting units, details or textual evidence


A number without its unit may be incomplete. “三十” could mean 30 minutes, yuan, kilometres or people. If the source says “三十分钟,” preserve the meaningful unit unless the question already makes it unmistakable and the response conventions permit omission.


The same principle applies beyond numerical units. A student may recognise the correct section of a text but submit an answer that is too broad. “Because it is convenient” is weaker than identifying what is convenient and why that matters. Conversely, copying an entire sentence can hide the relevant detail and may introduce information that contradicts the intended answer.


This is why advice drawn from IB Mandarin B examiner reports is most useful when converted into a checking habit. Reports and teacher feedback frequently focus on whether candidates have answered the precise question, developed relevant ideas and supported interpretation appropriately. However, the requirements vary by task and session. Use the latest materials supplied through your school to confirm the rules applying to your examination.


### The fix: use the answer-evidence check


For comprehension tasks, separate your thinking into two parts:


1. **Answer:** What is my direct response?
2. **Evidence:** Which word, phrase or detail proves it?


You may not need to write both parts separately, but you should be able to point to both. When a number appears, scan immediately for its classifier or unit. When the question requests multiple details, mark each completed element with a small tick during review.


### Losing marks through poor timing


Time pressure rarely arrives dramatically. It disappears in small decisions: rereading one paragraph again, polishing a sentence that was already clear, or refusing to leave a difficult item temporarily.


Lina might spend ten minutes trying to recover one uncertain answer. The cost is not only those ten minutes. It is the rushed writing, skipped checking and preventable character errors at the end.


Strong time management does not mean answering quickly. It means deciding where time has the greatest value.


### The fix: use checkpoints and controlled skipping


Divide the available time according to the sections and marks shown on your paper. Record two or three checkpoints, such as the time by which you should begin the final section and the time at which checking must start. Avoid creating a universal timing formula because SL and HL tasks, accommodations and examination materials can differ.


If an answer remains unclear after a reasonable attempt, mark it, move on and return later. Another question may reactivate the vocabulary or context you need. Reserve a final review window for omitted responses, units, evidence, audience, register and obvious character mistakes.


Timed practice matters because reading about timing cannot reproduce the feeling of a clock. RevisionDojo’s Questionbank lets you target weak skills, while Exam mode helps you sit timed papers under more realistic constraints. That combination teaches both knowledge and decision-making.


### Overcomplicating written responses


A further mistake is confusing complexity with quality. Students sometimes force memorised idioms, long linking phrases or advanced grammar into places where they do not fit. The result can sound unnatural or obscure an otherwise sensible idea.


Effective writing begins with purpose. Who is reading? Why are you writing? What response should the reader have? Once those questions are clear, vocabulary and grammar become tools rather than decorations.


The[overview of what Mandarin B is like](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-ib-mandarin-b-like) provides useful context for the course’s emphasis on meaningful communication. You can also strengthen flexible language through the broader[skills developed in Chinese B](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-skills-does-ib-chinese-b-develop) .


### The fix: prioritise clear, controlled Mandarin


Plan three things before writing: your main point, the evidence or example supporting it, and the appropriate register. Use ambitious language only when you can control it. Vary structures deliberately, but never sacrifice clarity to demonstrate a memorised phrase.


For oral preparation, the same rule applies. A rigid script can collapse when the conversation changes direction. The RevisionDojo guide to[preparing for the Chinese B individual oral](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-prepare-for-the-ib-chinese-b-individual-oral-exam) explains how structured but flexible preparation can work better.


### Turn each mistake into a repeatable drill


Mistake review becomes valuable only when it changes the next attempt. Keep a short error log with four columns: task, mistake, reason and new rule. “Lost a unit” becomes “circle every number and check its unit.” “Misread explain” becomes “rewrite every command term as an action before answering.”

Then return to the Questionbank for focused repetitions. The final lesson is reassuring. Avoidable mistakes are frustrating precisely because they are avoidable. You do not need a new personality or a perfect memory. You need a small set of actions practised often enough to remain available when the clock starts.
